Consider an \(n\)-indexed sequence of models with \(p=p(n)\) satisfying Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 and the \(\tau_n\)-condition. Define the statistics \(M_d,\tilde M_d\), the integers \(\ell_n,k_n\), and \(II_n=d_{\mathrm K}\big(\mathcal L(M_{k_n}),\mathcal L(\tilde M_{k_n})\big)\). We consider an \(n\)-indexed sequence of models with all parameters allowed to depend on \(n\) except those stated fixed; in particular \(p=p(n)\) may vary with \(n\), and constants not depending on \(n\) also do not depend on \(p\) in the source convention. Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\in\mathbb R^p\), \(S_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\mathbb E[X_i])\), with \(j\)th coordinate \(S_{n,j}\). Set \(\sigma_j^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_{1,j})\) for \(1\le j\le p\), ordered \(\sigma_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_{(p)}\) (these are standard deviations, not variances). Let \(\tau_n\in[0,1]\) and \(M=\max_{1\le j\le p}S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}\); let \(\tilde S_n\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) and \(\tilde M=\max_{1\le j\le p}\tilde S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}\). For random variables \(U,V\), \(d_{\mathrm K}(\mathcal L(U),\mathcal L(V))=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|\mathbb P(U\le t)-\mathbb P(V\le t)|\). For \(d\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), \(J(d)\) is a set of indices corresponding to the \(d\) largest values among \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p\) (tie-breaking not specified); \(R(d)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) is the correlation matrix of \(\{X_{1,j}:j\in J(d)\}\), and \(R^+(d)\) is its entrywise positive part \(R^+_{i,j}(d)=\max\{R_{i,j}(d),0\}\). Fix \(a\in(0,\tfrac12)\) not depending on \(n\), and set \(\ell_n=\lceil(1\vee\log(n)^3)\wedge p\rceil\), \(k_n=\lceil(\ell_n\vee n^{1/\log(n)^a})\wedge p\rceil\), so \(1\le\ell_n\le k_n\le p\) and both grow slower than any fractional power of \(n\). Define \(M_d=\max_{j\in J(d)}S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}\), \(\tilde M_d=\max_{j\in J(d)}\tilde S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}\), so \(M=M_p\), \(\tilde M=\tilde M_p\), and \(I_n=d_{\mathrm K}(\mathcal L(M_p),\mathcal L(M_{k_n}))\), \(II_n=d_{\mathrm K}(\mathcal L(M_{k_n}),\mathcal L(\tilde M_{k_n}))\), \(III_n=d_{\mathrm K}(\mathcal L(\tilde M_{k_n}),\mathcal L(\tilde M_p))\). The relation \(a_n\lesssim b_n\) means there exist \(c>0\) not depending on \(n\) and \(n_0\ge1\) such that \(a_n\le c\,b_n\) for all \(n\ge n_0\), the implied constant not depending on \(n\) nor on \(p=p(n)\). Assumption 2.1 (Data-generating model, A:model): (1) there exist \(\mu=\mu(n)\in\mathbb R^p\) and positive semidefinite \(\Sigma=\Sigma(n)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\) such that \(X_i=\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), where \(Z_1,\dots,Z_n\in\mathbb R^p\) are i.i.d.; (2) \(\mathbb E[Z_1]=0\), \(\mathbb E[Z_1Z_1^\top]=\mathbf I_p\), and \(\sup_{\|u\|_2=1}\|Z_1^\top u\|_{\psi_1}\le c_0\) for some \(c_0>0\) not depending on \(n\), where \(\|\xi\|_{\psi_1}=\inf\{t>0:\mathbb E[\exp(|\xi|/t)]\le2\}\) is the sub-exponential Orlicz norm; no constraint is placed on the ratio \(p/n\). Assumption 2.2 (Structural assumptions, A:cor): (1) \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p>0\) and there exist constants \(\alpha>0\), \(c>0\), \(c_\circ\in(0,1)\), not depending on \(n\), such that \(\sigma_{(j)}\le c\,j^{-\alpha}\) for all \(j\in\{k_n,\dots,p\}\) and \(\sigma_{(j)}\ge c_\circ\,j^{-\alpha}\) for all \(j\in\{1,\dots,k_n\}\); (2) there exists \(\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\), not depending on \(n\), such that \(\max_{i\ne j}R_{i,j}(\ell_n)\le1-\varepsilon_0\), \(R^+(\ell_n)\) with entries \(\max\{R_{i,j}(\ell_n),0\}\) is positive semidefinite, and there exists \(C>0\), not depending on \(n\), such that \(\sum_{1\le i<j\le\ell_n}R^+_{i,j}(\ell_n)\le C\ell_n\). The \(\tau_n\)-condition in both results requires \(\tau_n\in[0,1)\) and \((1-\tau_n)\sqrt{\log(n)}\gtrsim1\). The appendix convention that proofs may assume \(p>k_n\) is proof-level, not part of the displayed hypotheses of the propositions; if \(p\le k_n\), then the definition of \(k_n\) implies \(p=k_n\), hence \(I_n=III_n=0\).

Formalization clarifications from source and proof:
1. Constants and quantifier order (owner: Theorem 3.1, Section 2 “Setting and preliminaries,” and the Notation paragraph). The source explicitly treats a sequence of models indexed by \(n\): “all parameters depending on \(n\), except for those that are stated to be fixed,” with \(p=p(n)\), and it adds that “if a constant does not depend on \(n\), then it does not depend on \(p\) either.” Thus the intended reading of Theorem 3.1 is: fix \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and the fixed parameter \(a\in(0,1/2)\); consider an \(n\)-indexed model satisfying Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 and the \(\tau_n\) condition; the bound is an eventual \(n\to\infty\) statement. The \( \lesssim \) notation is defined by the source as the existence of a constant \(c>0\) not depending on \(n\), and \(n_0\ge1\), such that the inequality holds for all \(n\ge n_0\). Consequently the implicit constant in \(n^{-1/2+\delta}\) cannot depend on \(n\), cannot depend on \(p(n)\), and should not be allowed in Lean to depend on implicit parameters such as \(n,p,\Sigma,\sigma_j,R(d),J(d),\tau_n\), or the sample, merely because they are Lean parameters. The source only explicitly excludes dependence on \(n\); it does not explicitly list whether the implied constant may depend on fixed quantities such as \(\delta,a,\alpha,c,c_0,c_\circ,\varepsilon_0,C\), so that finer dependence is left unspecified and should not be invented. The constants \(c_0>0\) in Assumption 2.1, \(c>0\) and \(c_\circ\in(0,1)\) in Assumption 2.2(i), and \(C>0\) in Assumption 2.2(ii) are all stated to be “not depending on \(n\)”; \(c_0\) and \(c_\circ\) are different constants, and none of these is the hidden constant in \(\lesssim\). The condition “\((1-\tau_n)\sqrt{\log(n)}\gtrsim1\)” is itself an eventual lower-bound condition with a constant not depending on \(n\); it does not require \(\tau_n\) to be constant, only eventually not too close to \(1\). There is no theorem-level constant quantified after \(p\) or after a random vector in this result; if a proof introduces a constant after \(d\) or \(J(d)\), the source does not thereby make it uniform in \(d\) or \(p\) unless it says so.

2. Norms and mathematical objects (owner: Definitions and Assumptions of Theorem 3.1; Assumption 2.1). The only vector norm used in the selected theorem is the Euclidean \(\ell_2\) norm, written \(\|u\|_2\) in \(\sup_{\|u\|_2=1}\|Z_1^\top u\|_{\psi_1}\le c_0\). The Orlicz norm is explicitly defined in the Notation paragraph by \(\|\xi\|_{\psi_1}=\inf\{t>0:\mathbb E[\exp(|\xi|/t)]\le2\}\), and the condition applies to the scalar \(Z_1^\top u\) with \(u\) Euclidean unit. No sup norm, Frobenius norm, or operator norm replaces these objects in Theorem 3.1; the paper defines an operator norm elsewhere, but it is not part of this theorem’s hypotheses. The source defines \(\sigma_j^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_{1,j})\) and then writes \(\sigma_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_{(p)}\) as the “ordered standard deviations,” so \(\sigma_j\) and \(\sigma_{(j)}\) are standard deviations, not variances; the decay assumptions in Assumption 2.2 are on \(\sigma_{(j)}\), not \(\sigma_{(j)}^2\). The statistic \(S_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mathbb E[X_i])\) is already root-\(n\) scaled and centered by the population mean, and \(S_{n,j}\) is its coordinate. The Gaussian vector is \(\tilde S_n\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) with covariance \(\Sigma\), not \(\Sigma/n\); Assumption 2.1 only requires \(\Sigma\) positive semidefinite, so no full-rank condition should be added. The statistic \(M\) is the maximum of the scalar coordinates \(S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}\), not a vector norm, and \(\sigma_j>0\) from Assumption 2.2 makes the denominators meaningful; the exponent is \(\tau_n\in[0,1)\) in the theorem, although the preliminary definition says \([0,1]\). For \(J(d)\), the source says it is “a set of indices corresponding to the \(d\) largest values among \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p\),” and \(R(d)\) is the correlation matrix of the \(X_{1,j}\) with \(j\in J(d)\); the entries \(R_{i,j}(d)\) are entries in this \(d\times d\) local matrix, not automatically the original coordinate indices. The source calls \(R(d)\) a correlation matrix without displaying the entry formula; it should not be replaced by the covariance matrix, by a sample correlation, or by the correlation of \(Z_1\). The matrix \(R^+(d)\) has entrywise positive part \(\max\{R_{i,j}(d),0\}\); it is not the absolute-value matrix or \(R^\top R\). The source does not specify a tie-breaking rule for \(J(d)\) when the top \(d\) standard deviations are not unique; this is an unresolved ambiguity, and different tie choices could in principle change the displayed \(J(d),R(d),M_d,\widetilde M_d\) unless a deterministic convention is added.

3. Asymptotics (owner: Notation paragraph and Theorem 3.1). The source defines \(a_n\lesssim b_n\) for nonnegative sequences as: there exist \(c>0\) not depending on \(n\) and \(n_0\ge1\) such that \(a_n\le c\,b_n\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). Theorem 3.1 asserts the Kolmogorov-distance bound eventually in \(n\), with \(p=p(n)\) allowed to vary; it does not use \(O,o,\asymp\), or a probability qualifier. In particular, the theorem’s inequality is not an event holding with high probability; the high-probability statement belongs to the separate bootstrap theorem, not to Theorem 3.1. The asymptotic variable is \(n\), while \(p(n)\), \(\Sigma(n)\), the \(\sigma_j(n)\), \(R(d)\), and \(\tau_n\) may vary subject to Assumptions 2.1–2.2 and the \(\tau_n\) condition. The source explicitly says “no constraints are placed on the ratio \(p/n\)”; no such ratio condition should be added. The supplementary propositions labelled prop:bentkus and prop:IandIII use the same \(\lesssim\) convention and are proof-level supplement results; their inequalities for \(II_n\) and for \(I_n,III_n\) are not additional hypotheses of Theorem 3.1. The source does not fully specify the allowed dependence of the hidden asymptotic constants on the fixed constants or on \(\delta\), beyond excluding dependence on \(n\).

4. Potentially omitted definitions and side conditions (owner: Theorem 3.1 proof, Assumptions 2.1–2.2, and References R1–R2). \(\mathcal L(U)\) denotes the law, and \(d_{\mathrm K}\) is explicitly the supremum over scalar thresholds \(t\in\mathbb R\) of the absolute difference of CDFs, so it is not a vector-CDF distance. In Assumption 2.1, \(X_i=\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z_i\) with \(Z_1,\dots,Z_n\) i.i.d., \(\mathbb E[Z_1]=0\), \(\mathbb E[Z_1Z_1^\top]=\mathbf I_p\); there is no Gaussian requirement on \(Z_1\), and no constraint on \(p/n\). Assumption 2.2(i) requires all \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p\) positive and states the upper and lower decay bounds on the ranges \(\{k_n,\dots,p\}\) and \(\{1,\dots,k_n\}\), with overlap at \(k_n\), for constants independent of \(n\). The integers are defined using ceilings and \(\vee,\wedge\) by \(\ell_n=\lceil(1\vee\log(n)^3)\wedge p\rceil\) and \(k_n=\lceil(\ell_n\vee n^{1/\log(n)^a})\wedge p\rceil\), with \(a\in(0,1/2)\) fixed; the source leaves the logarithm base unspecified, and the notation \(\log(n)^3,\log(n)^a\) is naturally read as powers of \(\log n\). For \(d\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), \(M_d=\max_{j\in J(d)}S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}\) and \(\widetilde M_d=\max_{j\in J(d)}\widetilde S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}\), with \(M=M_p\) and \(\widetilde M=\widetilde M_p\). The proof writes \(I_n=d_K(\mathcal L(M_p),\mathcal L(M_{k_n}))\), \(II_n=d_K(\mathcal L(M_{k_n}),\mathcal L(\widetilde M_{k_n}))\), and \(III_n=d_K(\mathcal L(\widetilde M_{k_n}),\mathcal L(\widetilde M_p))\); these are proof-level definitions, not new hypotheses. The appendix conventions that \(n\) is sufficiently large and that proofs implicitly assume \(p>k_n\) are proof-level; the theorem itself should not acquire \(p>k_n\) as a hypothesis. The source notes that if \(p\le k_n\), then \(p=k_n\), so \(I_n=III_n=0\) and the proof reduces to \(II_n\). The supplemental results R1 (prop:bentkus) and R2 (prop:IandIII) are owned by the supplement proof of Theorem 3.1: R1 bounds \(II_n\), and R2 bounds \(I_n\) and \(III_n\), under the conditions of Theorem 3.1 as expanded there; they are not independent external universal theorems. External proof dependencies such as Bentkus’s multivariate Berry–Esseen theorem, Rosenthal’s inequality, and Slepian’s lemma are universal tools owned by those cited results; the target-specific variance-decay, \(J(d)\), and \(p>k_n\) conventions should not be imposed on the external theorem unless the local lemma explicitly restates them.

- `ellN p n := toNat( ⌈ min (max (1:ℝ) ((Real.log (n:ℝ))^3)) ((p:ℝ)) ⌉ )`,
- `kN p a n := toNat( ⌈ min (max ((ellN p n : ℕ) : ℝ) ((n:ℝ) ^ ((1:ℝ) / ((Real.log (n:ℝ))^a)))) ((p:ℝ)) ⌉ )`,

where `Real.log` is the real natural logarithm, `x ^ y` is real power, `⌈·⌉` is the integer ceiling and `toNat` is the nonnegative part of an integer, one has

`1 ≤ ellN p n`, `ellN p n ≤ kN p a n`, and `kN p a n ≤ p`.

Write `A₁ := min (max (1:ℝ) ((Real.log (n:ℝ))^3)) ((p:ℝ))` and `A₂ := min (max (((ellN p n : ℕ) : ℝ)) ((n:ℝ) ^ ((1:ℝ)/((Real.log (n:ℝ))^a)))) ((p:ℝ))`, so that `ellN p n = (⌈A₁⌉).toNat` and `kN p a n = (⌈A₂⌉).toNat`.

1. *Lower bound for `A₁`.* `max 1 ((Real.log (n:ℝ))^3) ≥ 1` and `(p:ℝ) ≥ 1` because `1 ≤ p`; a minimum of two numbers that are `≥ 1` is `≥ 1`. Hence `1 ≤ A₁` (and `A₁ > 0`). No information about the sign of `Real.log (n:ℝ)` is used, so `n = 0` and `n = 1` are covered.
2. *Upper bound for `A₁`.* `A₁ ≤ (p:ℝ)` because a minimum is at most its second argument.
3. *Ceiling.* From `1 ≤ A₁` and `A₁ ≤ ⌈A₁⌉` (`Int.le_ceil`) we get `1 ≤ ⌈A₁⌉`. From `A₁ ≤ (p:ℝ)`, `Int.ceil_le` (E44) with `z = (p:ℤ)` gives `⌈A₁⌉ ≤ (p:ℤ)`.
4. *`toNat`.* An integer `≥ 1` has `toNat ≥ 1` (`toNat` is monotone and `((1:ℤ)).toNat = 1`), so `1 ≤ (⌈A₁⌉).toNat = ellN p n`. Since `0 ≤ ⌈A₁⌉ ≤ (p:ℤ)` and `toNat` is monotone on nonnegative integers, `(⌈A₁⌉).toNat ≤ ((p:ℤ)).toNat = p`. This yields `1 ≤ ellN p n ≤ p`.
5. *The same for `A₂`.* By step 4, `((ellN p n : ℕ) : ℝ) ≥ 1`, and `(p:ℝ) ≥ 1`; hence `max (((ellN p n:ℕ):ℝ)) ((n:ℝ)^(1/(Real.log n)^a)) ≥ 1`, so `1 ≤ A₂`, while `A₂ ≤ (p:ℝ)`. Steps 3–4 applied verbatim to `A₂` give `1 ≤ kN p a n ≤ p`. (Again the real-power term is only ever compared with a `max` containing the already bounded quantity `ellN p n`, so no base/positivity condition on `n` or on the exponent is required.)
6. *Monotonicity in the first cut-off.* `A₂ ≥ min (((ellN p n:ℕ):ℝ)) ((p:ℝ)) = ((ellN p n:ℕ):ℝ)`, because a maximum dominates its first argument and `ellN p n ≤ p` by step 4. All reasoning is order theory on ℝ applied to the two real-valued functions `f(t) := |μ.real (Set.Iic t) − ρ.real (Set.Iic t)|` and `g(t) := |ρ.real (Set.Iic t) − ν.real (Set.Iic t)|`; no measurability, finiteness or σ-finiteness of μ, ν, ρ is used.

(Concretely `|a − b| ≤ 1` when `a, b ∈ [0,1]`.)

(b) *Boundedness of the two ranges.* By (a), `Set.range f ⊆ [0,1]` and `Set.range g ⊆ [0,1]`, so both ranges are bounded above (by the real number `1`). This is exactly the `BddAbove` input required by `le_ciSup` (E24).

(c) *Pointwise comparison with the suprema.* For each real `t`, `le_ciSup` (E24) applied to `f` with the boundedness from (b) gives `f(t) ≤ ⨆ s, f(s) = dK(μ,ρ)`, and applied to `g` gives `g(t) ≤ dK(ρ,ν)`.

(d) *Pointwise triangle inequality.* For each real `t`, the real triangle inequality for absolute values gives
`|μ.real (Iic t) − ν.real (Iic t)| = |(μ.real (Iic t) − ρ.real (Iic t)) + (ρ.real (Iic t) − ν.real (Iic t))| ≤ f(t) + g(t)`;
